transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Russian President Vladimir Putin says he won't negotiate
a ceasefire with Ukraine that covers
that country's energy infrastructure.
His remarks follow Kyiv's attack on a bridge
connecting Russia with Russian-occupied Crimea.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports from Kyiv.
Russian drones are targeting Kyiv
and air raid sirens wailed most of the day.
(thunder rumbling)
Explosions and the sound of air defense fire
rang out across the city.
NPR recorded the explosions while sheltering
inside its bureau.
Many buildings are damaged,
including the Austrian and Dutch embassies.
In a post on social media,
Ukraine's Foreign Minister urges the international community
to condemn Russia's "terror" in the boldest terms.
President Trump, meanwhile, was meeting
with Vladimir Putin in China,
where he greeted him warmly, calling him "my friend."
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kyiv.
Russian missile and drone attacks targeting Kyiv overnight
left at least three people dead.
President Trump is back in Washington
following his meetings in China.
He's expected to hold a news conference
at the White House this afternoon.
The Senate has passed legislation designed to make changes
to permitting in the energy sector.
As NPR's Julia Simon reports,
some democratic lawmakers and environmentalists
oppose the bill.
Proponents of the bill say that the current permitting
process is outdated, inefficient, and needs updates.
That is, easing of environmental regulations
and changes to laws
around building electrical transmission lines.
Some climate change advocates say the bill
will allow the country to build more solar,
wind, and battery projects.
And many climate scientists do agree
that the U.S. needs to speed up building
renewable energy projects and transmission lines.
But other democratic lawmakers oppose the bill.
They argue it will worsen climate pollution
by also making it easier to greenlight oil and gas projects
and energy-hungry data centers.
And they say it will weaken protections
for clean air and water.
Julia Simon, NPR News.
-Anthropic now holds the record
for an initial public offering of stock,
having raised more than $100 billion in its IPO.
NPR's John Ruich has more.
-IPOs are kind of a two-step process.
The company sells the shares at a fixed price to investors
who apply in advance to get in on the IPO.
That price was 83 bucks, which was higher than expected.
And then the shares start trading on the stock market,
and they started out with a bang,
opening up 34% from the IPO price.
Now, they've come down off of the high
over the course of the trading day,
but they did end trading still well above the IPO price.
-That's NPR's John Ruich.
Despite anthropic success,
investors mostly sold shares yesterday.
The Dow, the S&P 500, and the NASDAQ each lost more than 2%.
The Dow dropped more than 1,100 points.
This is NPR News.
Flooding remains an issue in areas of Florida
after days of heavy rains.
More than a foot of rain has fallen this week
in places such as Fort Lauderdale and Hollywood.
Plantation Florida near Miami has recorded
more than 16 inches of rain.
Roads and homes have flooded,
leaving some neighborhoods cut off.
Flood watches and warnings remain in effect
along the state's east coast
from Miami to north of Jacksonville.
An original handwritten draft of Martin Luther King, Jr.'s
"I Have a Dream" speech is on public display in Atlanta
before it's sold at auction.
Here's NPR's Debbie Elliott.
-The seven-page draft is written long hand on yellow legal paper
with sections scratched through and reworked.
It's on display through Sunday
at the Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta.
CEO Jill Savitt says it's a foundational artifact.
-Nothing has given me chills like this handwritten document
where you see him crafting one of the most iconic speeches
in U.S. history and the idea that this was a human being,
a man who sat down with a pen and a piece of paper,
struggling to find the right words.
-The draft was discovered in a desk drawer
by civil rights activist Zernona Clayton,
whose late husband was one of King's speech writers.
Debbie Elliott, NPR News, Atlanta.
-Freddy Mack says long-term mortgage rates in the U.S.
have gone up for the first time in more than a month.
The average 30-year fixed-rate loan
rose to more than 7.25% this week.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Putin rejects ceasefire covering Ukraine's energy infrastructure after Kyiv's Crimea bridge attack
Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv damage embassies and leave at least three dead
Trump greets Putin warmly in China, calling him 'my friend'
Senate passes bill easing energy permitting rules, opposed by Democrats and environmentalists
Anthropic's IPO raises over $100 billion, setting a record, with shares opening up 34%
Dow, S&P 500, and NASDAQ each fall more than 2% as investors sell stocks
Flooding persists in Florida after more than a foot of rain in Fort Lauderdale and Hollywood
Handwritten draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech on display in Atlanta before auction
Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rises above 7.25% for the first time in over a month
